title: Connection Pool Exhaustion
description: Diagnose and fix SQL Server connection pool exhaustion in ASP.NET Core applications by understanding pooling behavior, connection leaks, and correct async usage.

data.text: When every connection in the pool is in use, new requests wait—or fail with a timeout. **Connection pool exhaustion** is one of the most common production issues for data-driven ASP.NET Core apps. It usually stems from unclosed connections, long-running queries, or thread pool pressure that prevents connections from being returned quickly.
How SQL Server Connection Pooling Works

ADO.NET maintains a pool of physical connections per unique connection string. When you call `Open()`, it tries to borrow a connection from the pool. When you call `Close()` or `Dispose()`, the connection returns to the pool. If all connections are busy and the pool limit is reached, the call blocks until a connection is released or the connection timeout expires.

terms.definition: The maximum number of physical connections allowed in a pool. Defaults to 100 for SQL Server.
A connection that is opened but never closed or disposed, permanently removing it from the pool.
The time to wait for a connection from the pool before throwing a timeout exception. Defaults to 15 seconds.

data.title: Connection String with Pooling Settings
data.content: Configure pooling behavior explicitly in your connection string to match your workload.

data.text: Symptoms include `SqlException` timeout errors after 15–30 seconds, thread dump accumulation, and CPU spikes from blocked threads. Performance counters such as `.NET Data Provider for SqlServer` -> `NumberOfPooledConnections` and `NumberOfActiveConnections` reveal the pool state. You can also enable EF Core logging to see connection open and close events.

data.title: Logging Connection Events with EF Core
data.content: Configure EF Core to log when connections are opened and closed so you can spot leaks.

data.title: Connection Leaks Are Silent Killers
data.text: A single unclosed connection in a high-traffic loop will exhaust the pool in seconds. Always use `using` statements or dependency injection with scoped DbContext instances. Never cache a DbContext or SqlConnection in a singleton.

data.title: Fixes
items: Ensure DbContext is registered as scoped, not singleton or transient.
Keep queries short; long-running transactions hold connections longer.
Increase `Max Pool Size` only after confirming the workload genuinely needs more concurrent connections.

data.title: Key Takeaway
points: Connection pooling reuses physical connections, but only if you close or dispose them.
Monitor pool counters and EF Core logs to catch leaks before they cause outages.
The fix is almost always correct lifetime management, not a larger pool size.
data.takeaway: Pool exhaustion is a symptom of resource management bugs, not a configuration problem. Find the leak first.
